analysis.one_liner: Exempts corporate dividend income from federal income tax, phasing in to fully tax-free dividends by 2007.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a hearing, markup, or floor vote during the 2003-2005 Congress; it never received a vote in either chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed the tax code so that individuals no longer paid federal income tax on corporate dividends. It phased in through caps — $25,000 per person in 2003 rising to $100,000 in 2006, doubled for married couples — and after 2007 dividends would have been entirely tax-free. Because the benefit of a dividend tax cut depends entirely on how much stock someone owns, the money would have gone overwhelmingly to households in the top income brackets. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in January 2003 and was never scheduled for a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders who receive corporate dividends — and the benefit scales directly with how much stock a household owns. A household with no dividend income gains nothing, while a wealthy household drawing six figures in dividends could shelter the full amount from tax, with no cap at all starting in 2007. Publicly traded companies would also benefit indirectly, since tax-free dividends raise the value of their shares and make it cheaper for them to raise capital.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy shareholders with large dividend income

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Internal Revenue Code to exclude dividend income from gross income, meaning individuals would owe no federal income tax on most dividends they receive.
The exclusion phases in: a $25,000 cap per person in 2003, $50,000 in 2004, $75,000 in 2005, and $100,000 in 2006 (doubled on joint returns), with no cap at all starting in 2007.

Conforming amendments keep excluded dividends out of the earned income tax credit and count them for purposes of taxing Social Security benefits, so the exclusion would not accidentally boost those benefits or low-income credits for high earners.
The exclusion applies to individuals rather than to trusts and estates, which the conforming amendments require to still count excluded dividends in their income.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and through it every taxpayer. The revenue given up on dividend taxes would have to be replaced by borrowing (larger deficits), other taxes, or spending cuts — costs borne by people who own no stock at all.
analysis.who_pays_short: All taxpayers, via lost federal revenue

drawbacks.text: The federal government would give up tens of billions of dollars in annual revenue once dividends were fully tax-free from 2007, to be made up through borrowing, other taxes, or spending cuts.

The benefit scales with how much stock a household owns: because most dividend income flows to households in the top income brackets, the largest tax savings would go to the wealthiest shareholders, not to the typical family.

The bill left some dividends taxable on purpose — capital-gain dividends from mutual funds and real estate investment trusts, dividends from farmers' cooperatives, and dividends paid to employee stock ownership plans remain outside the exclusion.

Supporters would argue dividends are taxed twice (corporate profits are taxed at the company level, then again when paid to shareholders), and that removing the second layer would encourage investment — a real objection, though full exclusion is the costliest way to answer it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The strongest case for the bill was that corporate profits are taxed twice — once at the corporate level and again when paid out as dividends — and eliminating that double layer could make investing in U.S. companies more attractive. But a full exclusion from income is the most expensive possible way to address double taxation, and the benefit scales with how much stock a person owns, so the gains go overwhelmingly to households at the top. The bill would have cost the Treasury tens of billions of dollars a year once fully phased in, borne through deficits, other tax increases, or spending cuts, while offering little to the majority of households that receive no dividends at all. Weighing the honest cost, the design was badly proportioned to the problem it addressed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2003 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never scheduled it for a hearing or vote, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Wilson introduced the Dividend Taxation Elimination Act of 2003 on January 7, 2003.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the same day; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever appears in its action history.
The only later action in the record is the sponsor's introductory remarks in the House on March 13, 2003.
The bill's substance, as summarized by the Congressional Research Service, was to exclude dividends from gross income with specified exceptions and phase-in limits before 2007.
The bill had two cosponsors, both Republicans, and no further support in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Everyone who would otherwise have absorbed the cost of making dividends tax-free — through higher deficits, other tax increases, or spending cuts — is better off that the bill never reached the floor. Wealthy shareholders lost the full exclusion they would have gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary taxpayers; the bill never got a vote

for.name: Rep. Joe Wilson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 7, 2003 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor on March 13, 2003.

for.name: Two House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only two cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in January 2003 and took no recorded action: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no report to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and both of its cosponsors were Republicans, but it never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists of where either party stood.

industries.industry: Shareholders of publicly traded corporations, especially the wealthiest households
industries.note: Making dividends tax-free raises the after-tax return on stock ownership, and the gain scales directly with how many shares a household holds. Because the bulk of dividend income flows to top-bracket households, the largest dollar benefit goes to them, while the revenue is lost to everyone.

Tax-free dividends for their shareholders would raise the value of paying dividends and lower the cost of raising capital. The effect is mixed only in the sense that they would face no new obligation; their shareholders capture the direct gain.

The bill carves dividends from tax-exempt farmers' cooperative associations out of the exclusion, so those dividends would remain taxable even as other dividends became tax-free. A comparatively minor, technical effect.
